prompt: At the moment `COMMIT` returns, where is the new row guaranteed to be on disk?
hint: The lesson searched two places with grep.

choices.text: In a segment file under pg_wal, and nowhere else on disk yet
choices.why: Right. The commit waits for the log to reach the disk, and grep found the row there.

choices.text: In the table's own file under base/
choices.why: grep counted zero matches in the table's file after the commit: the page was still dirty in memory.

choices.text: In both the table's file and the log, written together
choices.why: Writing both at every commit is exactly the scattered write the log exists to avoid.

choices.text: Nowhere yet; it is still only in shared memory
choices.why: Then a power cut after COMMIT would lose it. The log record is on disk before the answer comes back.

prompt: Why is flushing the log at every commit cheaper than flushing the changed table pages?
hint: Think about where on the disk each write lands.

choices.text: The log is appended at its end, in one sequential write
choices.why: Right. One small sequential write instead of pages scattered across many files.

choices.text: The log is compressed and the pages are not
choices.why: Nothing is compressed by default; wal_compression is off. The difference is the shape of the write.

choices.text: The log lives in memory and is never written to disk
choices.why: The log is written to pg_wal, and grep found the row in a segment file there.

choices.text: Table pages are written by the session itself, which is slower than a background process
choices.why: It is the other way round: the session flushes the log, and background processes write the pages.

prompt: Match each process to what it writes.
hint: Two write the log, two write table pages.

pairs.right: its own WAL records, before COMMIT returns
every dirty page, at a checkpoint
a few dirty pages ahead of their memory being needed

prompt: The background writer is about to write a dirty page of `orders` whose last change is described at LSN 0/5000. The log is flushed only to 0/4000. What happens first?
hint: No page may reach its file before its description reaches the log.

choices.text: The page is written, and the log catches up at the next commit
choices.why: A crash between the two would leave a page on disk whose change the log does not describe.

choices.text: The page is skipped until a checkpoint writes it
choices.why: The checkpointer obeys the same rule; skipping does not remove the need to flush the log first.

choices.text: The server writes a full-page image of it into the log instead
choices.why: Full-page images go with the first change after a checkpoint, not with a page write.

choices.text: The log is flushed to at least 0/5000
choices.why: Right. That ordering is the write-ahead rule, enforced by the server before every page write.

prompt: What is an LSN such as `0/1584F1C0`?
hint: pg_wal_lsn_diff subtracts two of them and answers in bytes.

choices.text: A transaction id
choices.why: Transaction ids are the tx field in pg_waldump, 784 in the lesson. Many records share one.

choices.text: The name of the current segment file
choices.why: That is what pg_walfile_name turns an LSN into; the name has 24 digits, the LSN two halves.

choices.text: A timestamp in the server's internal clock format
choices.why: It is a position, not a time. The COMMIT record carries its time separately.

choices.text: A byte position in the log
choices.why: Right. Written in hexadecimal; subtracting two gives the bytes between them.

prompt: `pg_waldump` printed `blkref #0: rel 1663/16386/16420 blk 0`. Which file of the data directory did that record change?
hint: Tablespace, database, file; and 1663 is the default tablespace.

choices.why: Right. The same path pg_relation_filepath gave for notes, block 0 of it.
The record lives in pg_wal; blkref names the page it describes, which is elsewhere.
1663 is the tablespace, not a database. The database is the middle number.

choices.text: global/16420
choices.why: global holds tables shared by every database. A table of shop lives under base and shop's oid.

prompt: Which of the three records of one `INSERT` made the transaction durable?
hint: Without it, recovery treats the other two as belonging to a transaction that never finished.

choices.text: The Heap INSERT, because it holds the row
choices.why: The row's record alone belongs to an unfinished transaction until the commit record follows it.

choices.text: The Transaction COMMIT
choices.why: Right. Once that record is on disk, the transaction survives any crash.

choices.text: The Btree INSERT_LEAF
choices.why: That one puts the key into the index. It says nothing about whether the transaction finished.

choices.text: None of them; durability comes from the table file
choices.why: The table file did not contain the row when the commit returned. Durability came from the log.

prompt: On Ubuntu, `pg_waldump` is not on the PATH; it lives in /usr/lib/postgresql/16/___ with the server's own programs.
hint: The usual directory name for programs.

prompt: In `pg_waldump`, a record shows `len (rec/tot): 65/ 2877` and ends in `FPW`. What makes up most of the 2877?
hint: FPW stands for full-page write.

choices.text: The old and new versions of the row
choices.why: The second update of the same row was 78 bytes in total. Row versions are small.

choices.text: Every index entry the update had to change
choices.why: It was a HOT update, which changes no index; index entries would be records of their own.

choices.text: An image of the whole page, minus its unused middle
choices.why: Right. The record is 65 bytes; the rest is the page, minus its empty middle.

choices.text: Padding up to the next 8 kB boundary
choices.why: Records are not padded to a page; 2877 is not a multiple of anything.

prompt: Right after a CHECKPOINT, the lesson's first update of one order wrote 9176 bytes of WAL. How many bytes did the identical second update, made straight after it, write?
hint: No page image the second time.

prompt: Why does the first change to a page after a checkpoint carry an image of the whole page?
hint: What would a crash halfway through writing that page leave behind?

choices.text: So that replicas receive the page without asking for it
choices.why: Replicas replay the same records, but the image is there for recovery from a torn page, on any server.

choices.text: A torn page cannot be repaired by a small record
choices.why: Right. Recovery restores the image first, then applies the small records after it.

choices.text: Because the checkpoint deleted the page's earlier records
choices.why: Old segments are recycled, but the page itself is on disk after a checkpoint; the risk is the next write tearing it.

choices.text: To let VACUUM read the page from the log instead of the table
choices.why: Nothing reads pages from the log during normal work; the log is read at recovery and by replicas.

prompt: A nightly job rewrites one column of a 40 GB table, just after the checkpoint the job forces before it starts. Using the lesson's measurements, roughly how much WAL should you plan for?
hint: 66 MB of table wrote 234 MB the first time.

choices.text: About 40 GB, the size of the table
choices.why: The 66 MB copy wrote 234 MB, three and a half times its size: row records plus page images.

choices.text: Well over 100 GB, several times the table
choices.why: Right. At the lesson's ratio, about three and a half times the table, page images included.

choices.text: A few megabytes, since only one column changes
choices.why: Each row's update record carries the new row version, so the whole row is written again, a million times over.

choices.text: Under 40 GB, because the forced checkpoint removes the page images
choices.why: A checkpoint right before is what makes every first change carry an image.

prompt: Match each reader of the log to what it does with it.
hint: One mechanism, four uses.

pairs.right: replays since the last checkpoint, at start-up
replays records as they arrive, for ever
replays archived segments up to a chosen moment
turns records back into row changes

prompt: A colleague proposes `wal_level = minimal` to make bulk loads faster on a primary. What does the team give up?
hint: Which readers need more than crash recovery needs?

choices.text: Crash recovery
choices.why: minimal still records everything crash recovery needs. That is the level's whole definition.

choices.text: Nothing; it only changes how fast the walwriter wakes
choices.why: That is wal_writer_delay. wal_level decides what the records contain.

choices.text: Full-page writes, which minimal turns off
choices.why: full_page_writes is a separate setting and stays on at every wal_level.

choices.text: Any replica or archive built from this log
choices.why: Right. Some bulk operations skip the log entirely, so nothing downstream sees them.

prompt: The disk is full and `pg_wal` is the largest directory on it. What should you not do?
hint: Which files might hold the only copy of committed changes?

choices.text: Delete the oldest segment files by hand
choices.why: Right. They may hold changes not yet in the table files, and the server reads them at its next start.

choices.text: Look for an inactive replication slot
choices.why: That is the first check lesson 24 builds into the runbook, and it is safe.

choices.text: Read the server log for the last checkpoint line
choices.why: Reading changes nothing, and that line says what was recycled.

choices.text: Free space elsewhere on the same filesystem
choices.why: Removing files that are not the database's is a fair way to buy time.

prompt: After a checkpoint logged `25 recycled`, `du` showed `pg_wal` exactly as large as before. Why?
hint: What does recycling do to a file?

choices.text: du counts files that were deleted but still open
choices.why: du counts what is in the directory. Nothing was deleted: the line said 0 removed.

choices.text: The checkpoint failed and kept every segment
choices.why: It logged checkpoint complete. A failed one would not report what it recycled.

choices.text: max_wal_size reserves its full 1 GB in advance
choices.why: The directory was 417M, well under 1 GB. Nothing is reserved; segments are kept or removed.

choices.text: The files were renamed to be written over later
choices.why: Right. Recycled segments stay on disk under future names; removed ones would have freed space.

prompt: A replica was decommissioned last month. Since then `pg_wal` on the primary has grown every day. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: A promise that outlives whoever it was made to.

choices.text: max_wal_size is too small
choices.why: Too small a max_wal_size causes frequent checkpoints, not a directory that only grows.

choices.text: An inactive replication slot
choices.why: Right. The slot holds every segment from its position on, connected or not.

choices.text: wal_level was left at replica
choices.why: replica is the default and holds nothing back; it only decides what records contain.

choices.text: The walwriter stopped, so segments are never closed
choices.why: Segments are trimmed at checkpoints, by the checkpointer; the walwriter does not remove anything.

prompt: To check for a forgotten slot, query the view pg_replication___ and look for a row whose active column is false.
hint: The view lists every slot.

prompt: You set `max_slot_wal_keep_size = 50GB` on a primary with one replica. The replica is switched off for a week and the primary writes 80 GB of WAL meanwhile. What happens?
hint: The setting trades one failure for another.

choices.text: The primary stops accepting writes at 50 GB
choices.why: The limit is on what the slot may hold, not on writes; the primary keeps working.

choices.text: The primary's disk fills with 80 GB of WAL
choices.why: That is what happens with the default of -1. The setting exists to prevent it.

choices.text: The slot is given up and the replica must be rebuilt
choices.why: Right. The disk is protected, and the replica pays for it.

choices.text: The replica catches up from the 50 GB that was kept
choices.why: It needs every record since it stopped; with 30 GB of them gone it cannot replay past the gap.

prompt: Put in order what happens to one `UPDATE` that commits and later reaches its table file.
hint: Memory first, the table file last.
items: the page is changed in shared buffers
a record describing the change goes into the WAL buffers
the log is flushed to pg_wal
a checkpoint writes the page to its file
trap: COMMIT returning before the flush would be synchronous_commit = off, which lesson 8 measures.

prompt: You run `pg_wal_lsn_diff` around a one-row `UPDATE` twice, with no checkpoint between, and get 8300 bytes then 90. A colleague runs the same pair and gets 90 then 90. What best explains the difference?
hint: What had happened to that page since the last checkpoint, on each server?

choices.text: On their server the page had changed already since the checkpoint
choices.why: Right. The image is taken once per page per checkpoint cycle; their first update was not the first change.

choices.text: The colleague has full_page_writes off
choices.why: Possible in principle, but the setting is on by default, and the ordinary reason needs no misconfiguration.

choices.text: Their disk writes in 8 kB pieces
choices.why: PostgreSQL does not look at the disk to decide; the image rule depends only on the checkpoint.

choices.text: Their wal_level is minimal
choices.why: minimal still logs updates with full-page images; it only lets some bulk operations skip the log.

prompt: Two servers have the same data. Server A checkpoints every 30 seconds, server B every 15 minutes, under the same steady write load. Which writes more WAL per hour?
hint: Every checkpoint restarts the image rule for every page.

choices.text: Server A
choices.why: Right. Each of its checkpoints makes the next change of every page carry a full image again.

choices.text: Server B, because its checkpoints are larger
choices.why: A checkpoint writes table pages, not log. The log volume grows with images, which follow checkpoints.

choices.text: Both write the same, since the load is the same
choices.why: The same rows change, but how many changes are a page's first since a checkpoint differs.

prompt: Which of these read the write-ahead log? Choose all that apply.
hint: One mechanism, used four ways.

choices.text: A start-up after a crash
choices.why: Yes. It replays from the last checkpoint's redo point.

choices.text: A streaming replica
choices.why: Yes. It is a server replaying a log that keeps arriving.

choices.text: A SELECT on the primary
choices.why: Queries read pages from shared buffers and table files, never from pg_wal.

choices.text: A restore to a chosen moment
choices.why: Yes. A base backup plus archived segments, replayed to a record.

choices.text: autovacuum deciding which table to visit
choices.why: It decides from the statistics views, lesson 14, not from the log.

prompt: `pg_walfile_name(pg_current_wal_lsn())` answered `000000010000000000000015`. What does the leading `00000001` say?
hint: It changes when history branches.

choices.text: The timeline
choices.why: Right. It changes when a server is recovered to an earlier point or a replica is promoted.

choices.text: The database's oid
choices.why: Segments belong to the whole cluster, every database at once; the name carries no database.

choices.text: The first segment since the last restart
choices.why: Segment numbers continue across restarts; the last 16 digits are the segment number.

choices.text: The segment's version of the WAL format
choices.why: The format version is inside the files, not in their names.

prompt: To measure the WAL one statement writes, store the position before it with `SELECT pg_current_wal_lsn() AS before \gset`, run it, then call pg_wal_lsn___(pg_current_wal_lsn(), :'before').
hint: The function subtracts.
